idiom_name: originator-owned snapshot value + bounded caretaker behind a narrow interface
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: let the object that owns the state expose exactly two operations - create a snapshot value capturing the state it decides matters, and restore itself from such a snapshot - and keep the snapshot type opaque to everyone else. A separate caretaker (undo stack, command, transaction, form controller) stores snapshots and decides when to save or restore, but can only hold, count, label and discard them; it must never read or write their contents. Make the snapshot immutable and self-contained: copy the state rather than aliasing it, and include everything needed to re-establish the originator's invariants, not just the fields that changed. Bound the history by depth, age or memory, and discard snapshots whose originator is gone. When whole-state snapshots are too expensive, replace them with deltas or invertible commands, but keep the same narrow interface so the caretaker never learns the state's shape.
code_sketch:
m = originator.snapshot()          # opaque, immutable value
caretaker.push(m)                  # holds it, cannot read it
...
originator.restore(caretaker.pop())  # only the originator interprets it
pitfalls: A caretaker that reads or edits a snapshot has silently become a second owner of the state; keep the snapshot type private or behind a marker interface and expose metadata only.
A snapshot that aliases live state (a shallow copy) restores the present instead of the past - the classic silent no-op undo.
Neither the snapshot size nor the history depth is bounded: memory grows with every save.
Capturing open resources (file handles, sockets, DB connections) in the snapshot: restoration re-establishes a stale or invalid handle.
In dynamic languages, the caretaker can always introspect the memento through duck typing or attribute access regardless of naming conventions — the encapsulation guarantee is advisory only.
Mementos serialized to disk without schema versioning become unreadable after class evolution; plan for schema migration or use a stable serialization format.

Wrong move: Treat an inverse-action log as a full opaque snapshot -> undo fails when an operation omitted derived or externally changed state -> instead use an originator-owned snapshot for exact restoration, or label and validate command-based undo explicitly.

Wrong move: Apply a snapshot after the originator's schema or identity changed -> restore fails by placing stale state into the wrong instance -> instead validate originator identity, schema version and checksum before restore, then migrate or discard incompatible snapshots.

Wrong move: Assume a memento or database savepoint rolls back messages, files or network calls -> restore fails because external side effects escaped the captured state -> instead coordinate a transaction, outbox or compensating action and state the rollback boundary honestly.
